issues.failure_explanation: At a mixed-rank nonstationary point, nonstationarity means that at least one of the independent normal-cone conditions fails, not that both displayed residuals are positive. One residual can therefore vanish while the other is nonzero, making the minimum defining \bar{\delta} equal to zero. The subsequently defined \delta is then not positive, contrary to the proposition. Moreover, the proof branches according to whether the first projection term is exactly zero at a nearby candidate; when that term is merely nonzero but tends to zero, the first branch supplies no uniform positive lower bound from the second residual.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply a contained uniform lower-bound lemma that combines the two residual mechanisms without taking a possibly zero minimum and remains valid when the first projection term approaches zero; then redefine the positive decrease constant accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: Uniform sufficient decrease near mixed-rank nonstationary accumulation points is not established, so the GRAP-R apocalypse-free convergence theorem is unsupported in that regime.
issues.title: The mixed-rank decrease proof can define a zero decrease constant
issues.why_classification: The proof architecture may remain usable, but it needs a nontrivial new local uniform-bound argument covering the mixed-rank case rather than a routine algebraic correction.

issues.failure_explanation: The sufficient-decrease proposition formally assumes only full-rank reference points \underline{\tensX}\in\tensM_{\vecr}, whereas the theorem invokes it for arbitrary accumulation points, including rank-deficient ones. The attempted extra proof for deficient points does not close this gap: a nearby candidate may have rank strictly larger than the limiting rank, so its added singular subspaces need not converge to a fixed Tucker decomposition of the limit. In particular, an added factor direction can align with the relevant gradient component, causing the factor \proj_{\breve{\matu}_k}^{\perp} in \tilde{\proj}_k to annihilate that component; hence the asserted uniform one-half lower bound by the limiting partial direction does not follow from continuity.
